difficultyReason: Five conditional answer choices, any of which plausibly strengthens the argument; the correct answer must force the conclusion by closing the precise gap between 'a regulation is economically inefficient' and 'it ought to be repealed.' A reversed-conditional trap and a 'too weak' trap are both present, and a scope-shift trap trades on 'inefficient' versus 'harmful.' Students must trace the full conditional chain through the stimulus to identify which link is genuinely missing.
stimulus: A leading economist has argued that any environmental regulation that imposes costs exceeding its measurable benefits is economically inefficient. She further contends that the Clean Waterways Act, as currently structured, imposes costs that exceed its measurable benefits. On this basis she concludes that the Clean Waterways Act ought to be repealed.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any regulation that causes measurable economic harm to industry will eventually be repealed by the legislature.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any regulation that is economically inefficient ought to be repealed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Clean Waterways Act ought to be repealed only if a more cost-effective alternative regulation is available.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any regulation that ought to be repealed is one that imposes costs exceeding its measurable benefits.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulations that impose costs exceeding their measurable benefits tend to be unpopular and are often reconsidered by policymakers.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes two premises: (1) costs > measurable benefits → economically inefficient, and (2) the Clean Waterways Act has costs > measurable benefits. These together yield: the Act is economically inefficient. But the conclusion is that the Act ought to be repealed. The gap is 'economically inefficient → ought to be repealed.' Choice B supplies exactly that conditional, closing the chain to force the conclusion with logical necessity.
explanations.A: Scope shift trap. 'Causes measurable economic harm to industry' is different vocabulary from 'economically inefficient'; moreover, 'will eventually be repealed' is a prediction about what will happen, not a normative claim about what ought to happen — it cannot force a normative conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the missing conditional link: economically inefficient → ought to be repealed. Combined with the premises, it drives the conclusion to follow as a matter of logical necessity.
explanations.C: Reversed and conditional trap. This introduces a precondition (availability of an alternative) that, if anything, makes it harder to justify repeal. It also runs the conditional in the wrong direction relative to what the argument needs.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus needs 'inefficient → ought to be repealed'; choice D supplies the converse, 'ought to be repealed → costs exceed benefits.' This does not allow us to conclude the Act ought to be repealed merely because it is inefficient.
explanations.E: Too-weak trap. 'Tend to be unpopular' and 'often reconsidered' are probabilistic and descriptive; they do not logically force the normative conclusion that this particular Act ought to be repealed.
